transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-09-24 18:42 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-09-25T01:42:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 3.014 degrees and its azimuth is 266.753 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 6.78 degrees and its azimuth is 103.997 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 96.97 percent illuminated, 159.91 degrees from the Sun, and 385592.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes — very likely.

A 96.97%-illuminated Moon is essentially a bright gibbous Moon, and at only about 160° from the Sun it is on the opposite side of the sky from the low western Sun. With the Sun only ~3° above the western horizon, the sky around the Moon in the east-southeast should already be substantially darker than midday, even though it is still technically daylight.

At your time and location:

- **Look toward azimuth ~104°**: roughly **east-southeast**.
- The Moon is only **~6.8° above the horizon** — about the width of a clenched fist held at arm’s length, but a bit lower.
- It will be a very bright, nearly full-looking disk, though atmospheric haze, trees, buildings, or low terrain could easily hide it at that altitude.

The main limitation is not brightness but the **low elevation**. If you have a clear, unobstructed view of the ESE horizon, you should be able to spot it, probably quite readily. If the horizon is blocked or hazy, wait a little while: the Moon will climb while the Sun sets, making it dramatically easier to see.
